correctness.rationale: Let \(r\) be the number of terms whose denominators are pure powers of \(2\), and let \(S\) be their sum. Because the complete representation uses the odd prime \(p\), one has \(S<1\). After clearing the largest dyadic denominator, the positive dyadic gap \(1-S\) is at least \(2^{-r}\): a sum of \(r\) dyadic unit fractions below one cannot approach one more closely than the reciprocal of the product of its distinct binary place scales, and the standard common-denominator/popcount argument gives this bound exactly. Every remaining term is at most \(1/p\), so \(2^{-r}\le (R-r)/p\) and hence \(R\ge r+\lceil p/2^r\rceil\). Writing \(k=\lfloor\log_2 p\rfloor\), the cases \(r\ge k+1\), \(r=k\), and \(r\le k-1\) all yield \(R\ge k+2\). If \(p=2^k+1\) is prime, the explicit identity \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}2^{-j}+p^{-1}+(2^kp)^{-1}=1\) has rank \(k+2\), so the bound is sharp for every Fermat prime.
